physical_harm: The victim was found naked with blood oozing from her genitals, abrasions on her body, strangulation marks on her neck, and her hands tied with a sari. The medical evidence confirmed violent sexual intercourse and attempted strangulation leading to her death.
number_of_offences: Three offences (ss. 302, 376, and 392 IPC) were charged and finally upheld
financial_property_loss: The accused robbed various articles including jewellery and a VCR set from the deceased's house
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation as the accused tied the victim's hands, committed rape, and stole property from her house
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the chain of circumstantial evidence including oral evidence, post mortem report, evidence of the doctor who conducted the autopsy, medical examination of injuries on the accused, extra-judicial confession made to the doctor, forensic report, report of the Finger-Print Expert, and recoveries made from the house in occupation of the accused.
witness_credibility: All the witnesses who claimed to be present at or near the place of occurrence remained unshaken in cross-examination, thereby completing the chain of circumstantial evidence in a manner that clearly indicates that no one other than the accused committed the offences.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant-accused was apprehended by public for attempting similar offences two days after the incident in question.

legal_representation.accused: Kiran Suri, S.J. Amith, Ankolekar Gurudatta, Vijay Kumar Aparna Bhat
legal_representation.state: Anitha Shenoy, Rashmi Nandakumar, B.S. Gautham

appeal_history.high_court: Conviction upheld and death sentence confirmed

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused's conviction was based on circumstantial evidence which was complete and indicated that no one other than the accused committed the offences. They also emphasized the remorseless attitude of the accused, the manner in which the offences were committed, and the fact that the accused had committed similar offences before.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the conviction was based entirely on circumstantial evidence which was of no evidentiary value, and that the identification of the accused was questionable due to the publication of his photograph in the newspapers. They also submitted that the case did not fall within the 'rarest of rare cases' category.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a conviction based on circumstantial evidence is valid if it forms a complete chain of evidence that clearly indicates the guilt of the accused.
precedent_relied_upon: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684; Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (1983) 2 SCC 470; Musheer Khan alias Badshah Khan & Anr. Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh (2010) 2 SCC 748
sentencing_rationale: The death sentence was confirmed as the offences were committed with extreme depravity and the victim was killed in a merciless manner, bringing the case within the 'rarest of rare cases' category.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The accused's remorseless attitude, the violent and sexual nature of the offences, the fact that he had committed similar offences before, and the lack of remorse shown after the crime.
